Field surveys of the Collared iguanid lizard (Oplurus cuvieri) on the island of Grande Terre have provided robust morphometric data for this endemic species. Newly emerged hatchlings, having completed the process of yolk-sac resorption and initiated first exogenous feeding, possess a relatively modest body mass. Measurements taken from a cohort of neonates indicate that the initial wet weight at this stage is approximately 4.2 grams [Ww0 = approximately 4.2 grams], a value that reflects the substantial yolk reserves contained within the parchment-shelled egg from which they emerged. Hatchlings begin actively foraging for small arthropods shortly after shell pipping and nest emergence, commencing a rapid phase of mass gain. The incubation period required for the cleidoic, leathery-shelled eggs to reach the point of eclosion has been studied under controlled laboratory conditions. At a constant incubation temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C], the duration from oviposition to hatching, or age at birth, was recorded as 74 days [ab = 74 days], which is consistent with the developmental tempo observed in several other iguanid species from similar tropical environments.

As juvenile Oplurus cuvieri progress through successive sheds, they undergo a pronounced shift in body proportions, with snout-vent length (SVL) increasing steadily during the first year of post-hatching life. Growth trajectories derived from mark-recapture data indicate that the onset of gonadal maturation is tied to the attainment of a specific body size rather than a strict chronological age. Puberty, defined by the initial signs of gametogenesis onset and reproductive activation, is typically achieved when individuals reach a SVL at puberty of 5.5 centimeters [Lp = 5.5 centimeters]. This size threshold is reached by young iguanas after approximately 365 days since birth [tp = approximately 365 days since birth] when reared under thermal conditions averaging 29 °C [T = 29 °C]. The correspondence between this size-based trigger and the time-based metric suggests that somatic growth rate is the primary determinant of sexual maturation timing in this species, an interpretation supported by observations of slower-growing individuals that delay reproductive activation until they surpass the requisite body length.

Reproduction in Oplurus cuvieri is strongly seasonal, with females producing a single clutch of eggs each year during the austral summer. Data from a long-term field study indicate that gravid females, identifiable by their distended abdomens prior to oviposition, exhibit a maximum clutch frequency under optimal thermal regimes. At a mean ambient temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the maximum clutch frequency for this species is one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], with each clutch containing an average of 4 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing an average of 4 eggs]. This translates to a modest annual fecundity when compared to smaller, more r-selected lizard species. The thermal dependence of reproductive physiology is also evident in the relationship between temperature and lifespan; the maximum lifespan recorded for wild individuals under field conditions at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] is approximately 9.3 years [am = approximately 9.3 years], a longevity that positions Oplurus cuvieri as a relatively slow-living species within the Opluridae family.

Adult females of the Collared iguanid lizard achieve a substantially larger body size than males, a pattern of sexual size dimorphism that is common among many iguanid taxa. The ultimate wet weight for females, representing the maximum recorded body mass attained by reproductively active adults at the end of the growth period, has been documented at 114.63 grams [Wwi = 114.63 grams], far exceeding the typical 80 to 90 grams observed in adult males, which prioritize territorial defense and mate acquisition over somatic bulk. This asymptotic mass, measured from a sample of post-pubertal females during the peak of the breeding season, reflects the considerable energetic investment required for vitellogenesis and the production of a full complement of yolked eggs. The ultimate SVL of the species, or the asymptotic snout-vent length reached by fully grown individuals, has been estimated at 10 centimeters [Li = 10 centimeters], based on a total length of 35 centimeters, with females generally approaching the upper end of this length range.

The ecological strategy of Oplurus cuvieri is characterized by a slow pace of life, with delayed maturation, modest annual reproductive output, and extended longevity relative to many other small-bodied reptiles occupying comparable niches. The physiological underpinnings of this life-history syndrome are reflected in the species' metabolic and thermoregulatory biology. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the maximum lifespan of approximately 9.3 years [am = approximately 9.3 years] observed in Oplurus cuvieri at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] may be attributable, in part, to a relatively low resting metabolic rate that reduces cumulative oxidative damage over time. The timing of first reproduction, which is closely aligned with the attainment of a 5.5 centimeter [Lp = 5.5 centimeter] SVL and occurs roughly one year after hatching  at 29 °C [T = 29 °C], further underscores the species' conservative strategy of prioritizing growth before reproductive investment, a pattern that maximizes lifetime fitness in the stable, resource-limited environments of the dry forests it inhabits.
